title: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation for LLM Infra
desc: The formulas you do on a napkin before you provision a single GPU: memory footprint, KV cache growth, throughput, cost per token, and retry-storm headroom.
content:
Why Envelope Math Comes Before Any Config File

Before you touch --tensor-parallel-size or price out an EC2 instance, you should be able to answer five questions on a napkin: does the model fit in VRAM, how much room is left for KV cache, how many concurrent requests can you actually serve, what does a million tokens cost, and how much extra headroom do you need so a wave of retries doesn't tip the cluster over. Get these wrong and you either overpay for idle GPUs or discover your outage during a traffic spike.

Memory footprint KV cache sizing Little's Law Roofline throughput Cost per token Backoff headroom

1. Model Memory Footprint

The first constraint is trivial but non-negotiable: the weights have to fit in VRAM before anything else does.

Weight memory
VRAMweights = params × bytes_per_param × (1 + overhead)

Overhead (CUDA context, activations at rest, framework buffers) is typically 5–10%. bytes_per_param is 2 for fp16/bf16, 1 for int8, 0.5 for int4 (AWQ/GPTQ).

ModelParamsfp16int8int4
Llama-3 8B8B~16 GB~8 GB~4 GB
Llama-3 70B70B~140 GB~70 GB~35 GB
⚠️
70B at fp16 needs 2×A100-80GB minimum
140 GB of weights alone exceeds a single 80 GB GPU — before you've allocated a single byte of KV cache. This is why 70B-class models are almost always served with tensor parallelism across 2–4 GPUs, or quantized to int4 to fit on one.

2. KV Cache: The Memory That Grows With Every Request

Weights are fixed. KV cache is not — it grows with context length and with how many sequences you serve concurrently, and it competes for the same VRAM.

KV cache size (bytes)
KV = 2 × L × Hkv × D × S × B × b

Where L = layers, H_kv = KV heads (fewer than attention heads under GQA/MQA), D = head dimension, S = sequence length, B = batch size (concurrent sequences), b = bytes per element (2 for fp16). The leading 2 accounts for storing both K and V.

Python · envelope calculator
def kv_cache_bytes(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, seq_len, batch, bytes_per_elem=2):
    return 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * seq_len * batch * bytes_per_elem

# Llama-3 8B: 32 layers, 8 KV heads (GQA), head_dim 128
per_seq_4k = kv_cache_bytes(32, 8, 128, 4096, batch=1)
print(f"KV per 4k-token sequence: {per_seq_4k / 1e9:.2f} GB")  # ~0.54 GB

def max_batch_for_budget(vram_budget_gb, weight_gb, layers, kv_heads, head_dim, seq_len):
    free_bytes = (vram_budget_gb - weight_gb) * 1e9
    per_seq = kv_cache_bytes(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, seq_len, batch=1)
    return int(free_bytes // per_seq)

# 80GB A100, 16GB weights, 4k context -> how many concurrent sequences fit?
print(max_batch_for_budget(80, 16, 32, 8, 128, 4096))  # ~119 sequences
KV cache scales linearly with both sequence length and concurrent batch size — it is usually the binding constraint on an 80 GB GPU, not the weights.

3. Little's Law: Sizing Concurrency

Queueing theory gives you the relationship between throughput, latency, and how many requests you must be able to hold in flight.

Little's Law
L = λ × W

L = average number of requests in the system (concurrency), λ = arrival rate (requests/sec), W = average time each request spends in the system (queue + service). If you expect 50 req/s and each takes 2s end-to-end, you need to sustain L = 100 concurrent sequences — that's your floor for max-num-seqs, not a nice-to-have.

📐
Under-provisioning L shows up as queueing, not errors
If your engine's max concurrent sequences is below the Little's-Law floor, requests queue silently and W balloons — often the first symptom is TTFT p99 creeping up with no matching error-rate spike.

4. Roofline Throughput: Compute-Bound vs Memory-Bound

Transformer inference has two phases with opposite bottlenecks. Prefill (processing the prompt) is compute-bound — it does one matmul pass over many tokens, so it scales with GPU FLOPs. Decode (generating one token at a time) is memory-bandwidth-bound — each step re-reads the entire weight matrix from HBM for a single token, so it scales with GPU memory bandwidth, not FLOPs.

Roofline estimate
tokens/sec ≈ min( FLOPsgpu / FLOPsper-token , BWgpu / bytesread-per-token )

Roughly: FLOPs_per_token ≈ 2 × params, and per-token decode reads roughly the full weight tensor (bytes_read_per_token ≈ params × bytes_per_param). On an A100 (312 TFLOPS bf16, 2 TB/s HBM), an 8B model is memory-bound in decode: 2 TB/s ÷ (8e9 × 2 bytes) ≈ 125 tokens/sec/stream ceiling, which is why batching many concurrent decodes (to amortize that same weight read) is the entire point of continuous batching.

5. Cost Per Token

Cost per 1M tokens
cost = (GPU_hourly_price / (tokens_per_sec_sustained × 3600)) × 1,000,000

Example: an on-demand g5.12xlarge (4×A10G) at ~$5.67/hr sustaining 2,000 output tokens/sec aggregate across a batched vLLM deployment: (5.67 / (2000 × 3600)) × 1e6 ≈ $0.79 per 1M output tokens — before accounting for input-token prefill cost and idle capacity. Always benchmark sustained throughput under realistic concurrency (Day 6) rather than single-stream numbers; single-stream throughput overstates cost efficiency by 5–10x.

6. Backoff Envelope: Headroom for Retry Storms

Capacity math so far assumes steady-state traffic. Real systems retry on timeouts and 5xxs, and a partial outage can turn N req/s of real traffic into 2-3N req/s of combined real-plus-retry traffic right when the system is already struggling.

Exponential backoff with jitter
delay = min(cap, base × 2attempt) × random(0, 1)

Full jitter (AWS's recommended form) prevents synchronized retry waves — without it, every client backs off in lockstep and re-hammers the cluster at the same instant. For capacity planning, budget headroom: if your retry policy allows up to 2 retries per request and 5% of requests fail on first attempt, provision for ~1.1× the steady-state L from Little's Law, not exactly L — that margin is what keeps a bad minute from cascading into a bad hour.

Key Takeaways
1. Weight memory is fixed; KV cache is the variable that actually determines how many concurrent users you can serve. 2. Little's Law (L = λW) turns your traffic forecast into a concrete max-num-seqs floor. 3. Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, which is why continuous batching — not raw GPU FLOPs — is the main throughput lever. 4. Always provision ~10% extra concurrency headroom for retry storms; steady-state math alone under-provisions for failure conditions.
